articles.title: WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1: What Changed and What to Re-Test
articles.excerpt: Originally published at AccessGuard. If your site was built or audited against WCAG 2.1 and someone now asks for WCAG 2.2, the good news is that the gap is small and well defined. WCAG 2.2 keeps every…
articles.body: Originally published at AccessGuard . If your site was built or audited against WCAG 2.1 and someone now asks for WCAG 2.2, the good news is that the gap is small and well defined. WCAG 2.2 keeps every WCAG 2.1 success criterion except one, adds nine new ones, and changes nothing about color contrast. This guide covers only the difference: what was added, what was removed, which of it applies at Level AA, and what a team that already meets 2.1 has to re-test. Every level and quotation below comes from the WCAG 2.2 Recommendation (current edition dated 12 December 2024) and its Comparison with WCAG 2.1 section. If you want the full list of Level A and AA criteria instead, use our WCAG 2.2 checklist .
articles.author: Denis Omerovic

articles.title: Why Does My Phone Security Camera Show Less of the Room? Video Stabilization Crops the Edges, and a Fixed Camera Doesn't Need It
articles.excerpt: You prop an old Android phone on a shelf, open the normal camera app, and the whole doorway fits in the frame. Then you start recording for real, look at the clip later, and the edges are gone. The do…
articles.body: You prop an old Android phone on a shelf, open the normal camera app, and the whole doorway fits in the frame. Then you start recording for real, look at the clip later, and the edges are gone. The door frame is cut off. The corner where the delivery person stood is just outside the picture. Nothing moved. The phone did not slip. One common cause is a setting most people never think about on a camera that sits still: video stabilization . This article explains what Android's own documentation says stabilization does to the picture, how much of the frame it is allowed to take, and why a phone used as a fixed, offline security camera usually gains nothing from it.

articles.body: In part 1 I built price-level alerts that fire once and re-arm. Price is the easy signal. The more interesting one is money moving : a 500 BTC transfer, or a wallet you care about suddenly sending funds. Big transfers don't predict price, but they're a useful "look now" signal. Coins moving towards exchanges can mean someone is preparing to sell, and a dormant wallet waking up is worth knowing about. Here's how I watch both in n8n with no API keys, and why I eventually moved part of it out of n8n. The same skeleton as part 1 Schedule → Config (Set) → Check (Code) → Notify (Code) Config holds the thresholds and the Telegram/Discord settings, Check does the work and keeps state, and Notify sends every item's text to Telegram and/or Discord (dry-run if tokens are empty).

articles.title: HBM3E at High Bandwidth: Why the Power Network Matters as Much as the GPU
articles.excerpt: HBM3E systems are often described by bandwidth and stack capacity, but the practical limit is just as often the power network around the accelerator. A package can have enough compute and memory bandw…
articles.body: HBM3E systems are often described by bandwidth and stack capacity, but the practical limit is just as often the power network around the accelerator. A package can have enough compute and memory bandwidth yet still miss its operating target because the voltage rail moves too far during a burst, the interposer runs hot, or the board cannot remove the heat from dozens of tightly packed regulators and capacitors. The design answer is to treat HBM3E power delivery as a control, layout, thermal, and verification problem from the first architecture review. Why is HBM3E power delivery difficult? An accelerator with HBM3E does not draw a smooth, slowly changing load. Matrix engines, memory controllers, and fabric links change activity on short time scales.

articles.title: Europe's Space Rider vehicle comes crashing down during drop test
articles.excerpt: The full-scale prototype of Europe's Space Rider orbiter failed to deploy its parachute during a drop test earlier this month, but ESA officials hope the setback won't delay progress toward its first…
articles.body: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of "Star Trek." Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight.
